title: War-Damaged Gaza Apartment Block Collapses, Killing at Least 20
excerpt: The al-Sa'ada building in Gaza City's Rimal neighborhood collapsed overnight with about 100 people believed trapped, exposing the perilous living conditions of displaced Palestinians as reconstruction remains stalled.
body:
• At least 20 Palestinians, including several children, were killed when a war-damaged apartment building collapsed overnight in Gaza City; around 100 more people are believed trapped under the rubble.
  • The al-Sa'ada building in the Rimal neighborhood had been weakened by Israeli airstrikes at the start of the war. At least 10 displaced families were sheltering inside a structure rescue workers knew was unstable.
  • Rescuers are digging mostly by hand. Egypt has sent heavy machinery, the UAE and Qatar are delivering relief items, and UN agencies have deployed equipment and workers.
  • Tens of thousands of Palestinians live in roughly 2,000 buildings damaged by strikes across Gaza; the UN says about 400 structures are at risk of collapse, with winter rains approaching.

Gaza's civil defence pulled bodies from the wreckage of a bombed-out apartment building in Gaza City on Wednesday after it collapsed overnight, killing at least 20 Palestinians — including children — and trapping dozens of others beneath layers of rubble.

The six-storey al-Sa'ada building in the city's Rimal neighborhood, damaged by Israeli airstrikes at the beginning of the war, gave way as families slept, according to local authorities and wire reports. Reuters reported at least 20 dead, including six children, with 14 injured; CNN cited the director of al-Shifa hospital saying at least 21 had been killed, including 11 children; the Associated Press put the toll at 21 dead, including 11 children and five women.

Gaza's Civil Defense agency said around 100 people remained missing at the site, and rescue teams were working largely without heavy machinery to reach anyone still alive.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble."

— Raed Al-Dahshan, Director of Gaza City's Civil Defence

A collapse rescuers saw coming

The building was known to be unstable. It had been hit by Israeli strikes in the early days of the war that followed the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, and around six displaced Palestinian families were sheltering there despite knowing it was on the brink of collapse.

"The lack of options and alternatives left them with no other choice," said Aboud Majdalawi, a civil defense rescuer. The UN's humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Ramiz Alakbarov, said roughly 100 people, including 50 children, had been living in the building. "I am devastated by reports of people trapped under the rubble," he said.

Living among ruins

The disaster points to the scale of Gaza's shelter crisis. Tens of thousands of Palestinians are living in some 2,000 buildings damaged by strikes across Gaza, according to Reuters. The UN estimates around 80% of all structures in the territory have been damaged since the conflict began, with two-thirds destroyed, and some 1.9 million Palestinians — about 90% of the population — have been displaced, many of them multiple times.

Hamas' media office in Gaza said the building fell onto "dozens of displaced families who had been forcibly driven to seek shelter there, amid the complete absence of alternative and safe places of refuge."

"The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed. So there are actually people that are digging with their bare hands."

— Alessandro Mrakic, Head of UNDP's Gaza Office

No reconstruction in sight

No reconstruction work has taken place since a ceasefire was agreed to almost a year ago, the AP reported. Israel has said it will not permit rebuilding until Hamas disarms, and only a handful of excavators have been allowed into Gaza. Mrakic, head of the UN Development Programme's Gaza office, said some UN agencies had joined the rescue effort, which he described as difficult due to the lack of proper machinery; Egypt's relief agency was also assisting.

Egypt has provided heavy machinery while the United Arab Emirates and Qatar are set to deliver relief items, the UN said, and the UNDP has deployed available machinery and workers to support rescue efforts and survivors.

What to watch

The immediate question is whether anyone remains alive under the rubble. Beyond that, the UN warns of a wider threat: Mrakic said roughly 400 buildings in Gaza are at risk of collapse, and with winter approaching, rain could bring more of them down. "We know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he said.

For readers following the war's humanitarian toll, the collapse is a reminder of how Gaza's destruction continues to claim lives well beyond the battlefield — through the damaged buildings displaced families are forced to shelter in.
